properties.name: Al Wahbah crater
properties.description: A maar about 2 km wide and 250 m deep at the edge of Harrat Kishb, blasted through Precambrian basement by a phreatomagmatic eruption when rising basalt met groundwater. Its floor is a white evaporite pan of sodium-carbonate and salt crusts.
properties.photo_caption: Al Wahbah maar with its white evaporite floor

properties.name: Wabar impact craters
properties.description: A field of small impact craters in the eastern Rub' al Khali, formed when an iron meteorite struck loose dune sand in the late Holocene. The site is known for black impact glass, white shock-lithified sand ('instant rock') and iron-nickel fragments, now partly buried by migrating dunes.

properties.name: North Riyadh UNESCO Global Geopark: Edge of the World
properties.description: Here the Tuwaiq escarpment drops about 300 m in vertical cliffs of Upper Jurassic Tuwaiq Mountain and Jubaila limestones to the plain below. The cliffs expose a shallow-marine carbonate succession that dips gently east beneath Riyadh and the Arabian Platform.
properties.photo_caption: Jurassic limestone cliffs at the Edge of the World

properties.name: Salma UNESCO Global Geopark (Ha'il)
properties.description: Jabal Salma is a cluster of granite inselbergs in the northern Arabian Shield: late Neoproterozoic post-orogenic granites exhumed from beneath the Paleozoic cover. Exfoliation domes, tafoni and boulder fields rise several hundred metres above the surrounding pediment.

properties.name: Jabal Qidr (Harrat Khaybar)
properties.description: A young basaltic stratocone in Harrat Khaybar with dark, little-weathered lava flows that run several kilometres across older lavas. Nearby Jabal Abyad, a pale trachyte–comendite dome, shows the evolved end of the same volcanic system.
properties.photo_caption: Satellite view of Harrat Khaybar: the pale Jabal Abyad dome among dark lava flows

properties.name: Umm Jirsan lava tube
properties.description: One of the longest lava tubes in Arabia, about 1.5 km long, formed inside a pahoehoe basalt flow of Harrat Khaybar when the crust froze over a draining lava channel. Its collapse skylights and lava levees are well preserved on the surface.

properties.name: AlUla sandstone landscapes
properties.description: Cambrian–Ordovician fluvial and shallow-marine sandstones lie unconformably on the Precambrian Shield and are eroded into towers, arches and isolated buttes. Wind and salt weathering have cut overhangs and alcoves, as at Elephant Rock and the tombs of Hegra.
properties.photo_caption: Elephant Rock: an eroded remnant of Cambrian–Ordovician sandstone

properties.name: Wadi Disah
properties.description: A deep, palm-filled canyon cut into Cambrian–Ordovician sandstones on the north-western edge of the Shield. Springs fed by the sandstone aquifer keep water at the surface, between near-vertical walls several hundred metres high.
properties.photo_caption: Sandstone walls and palms in Wadi Disah

properties.name: Farasan Islands
properties.description: Low islands of uplifted Quaternary coral reef and lagoonal limestone on the Red Sea shelf off Jazan. They are pushed up by Miocene salt diapirs rising from the evaporites of the Red Sea rift fill.
properties.photo_caption: Raised reef limestone on the Farasan coast

properties.name: Jabal Al-Qarah (Al-Ahsa)
properties.description: A flat-topped mesa of Neogene (Hofuf Formation) sandy marl and limestone at the edge of the Al-Ahsa oasis, within the UNESCO World Heritage site. Narrow solution and joint-controlled caves stay cool year round.

properties.name: Wadi Ghul and Jebel Shams
properties.description: Oman's 'Grand Canyon' is incised about 1,000 m into Permian–Cretaceous shelf carbonates of the Jebel Akhdar dome, beneath Jebel Shams, the highest summit of the Hajar Mountains. The walls expose the autochthonous platform that underlies the Semail ophiolite nappes.
properties.photo_caption: Wadi Ghul (Wadi an Nakhur) below Jebel Shams

properties.name: Al Hoota Cave
properties.description: A karst cave of about 4.5 km in Mesozoic limestones on the flank of the Jebel Akhdar dome, with a subterranean lake and speleothems. It records cave formation as the dome was uplifted and dissected in the Neogene.
properties.photo_caption: Limestone cliff and the entrance to Al Hoota Cave

properties.name: Bimmah sinkhole
properties.description: A collapse doline about 50 m across and 20 m deep in Paleogene limestone near the coast, floored by brackish water fed by seawater and groundwater. It formed by dissolution of the limestone and collapse of the cave roof.

properties.name: Wahiba Sands
properties.description: A sand sea of north–south megaridges up to about 100 m high between the Hajar Mountains and the Arabian Sea. Older lithified Pleistocene eolianites underlie the active dunes and record past monsoon climates.

properties.name: Jebel Hafeet
properties.description: An elongate anticline of Paleogene limestones about 1,250 m high on the foreland of the Oman mountains, near Al Ain. Folding is related to the Neogene Zagros/Oman compression, and its flanks are rich in nummulites and other marine fossils.
properties.photo_caption: Aerial view of the Jebel Hafeet anticline

properties.name: Zekreet mesas
properties.description: Mushroom-shaped mesas and buttes of Eocene–Miocene limestone on the west coast of Qatar, carved by wind abrasion and salt weathering. Resistant caps protect softer marls below, producing undercut pedestals.
properties.photo_caption: A wind-carved limestone mushroom rock at Zekreet

properties.name: Jebel ad Dukhan (Bahrain)
properties.description: The highest point of Bahrain (about 135 m) sits at the centre of a broad domal anticline whose concentric rims of Paleogene limestone ring a central depression. The dome is one of the clearest surface expressions of a Gulf salt-cored structure.

properties.name: Jal Az-Zor escarpment
properties.description: A Neogene escarpment that rises about 140 m along the north shore of Kuwait Bay, cut in fluvial sandstones and gravels of the Dibdibba and Fars formations. It is Kuwait's main relief feature and a known site for Miocene vertebrate fossils.

properties.name: Wadi Hadramawt
properties.description: A canyon system about 300 m deep cut into the flat-lying Paleocene–Eocene limestone plateau (the Jol) of southern Yemen. Its near-vertical walls follow the layering of the shelf carbonates, which is why the plateau surface is so uniform.
properties.photo_caption: Wadi Hadramawt below the limestone plateau
